title: Wollstonecraft's Rights of Woman
objective: After this level you can explain why Mary Wollstonecraft argued in 1792 that women seem less rational only because they are denied education.
summary: Wollstonecraft (1792) answered Rousseau’s Emile: a false system of education, not nature, made women seem less rational, so women should be educated to reason.

cards.headline: What if women only seemed less rational because nobody let them learn to reason?
cards.body: In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft made exactly that argument, and aimed it at one of the most admired writers of her century.

cards.headline: Rousseau’s Sophie
cards.body: In Emile (1762), Jean-Jacques Rousseau argued that since men and women are not made alike, they should not be educated alike. His heroine Sophie is educated to please her husband, Emile. Revolutionary France had its own version: Talleyrand’s plan for French schools offered girls only a domestic education. Wollstonecraft’s Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792) answered both.

cards.headline: A false system of education
cards.body: The weakness people saw in women, Wollstonecraft replied, was manufactured. She blamed “a false system of education,” written by men more anxious to make women alluring than rational. Girls were taught that beauty is woman’s sceptre, and so the mind, “roaming round its gilt cage, only seeks to adorn its prison.” Change the schooling, and you change the woman it produces.

cards.headline: What she asked for
cards.body: The Vindication wanted women educated to be rational and self-governing. Women should learn skills to support themselves, so no one had to marry for money, and she even floated women having elected representatives of their own. Her quarrel was with the schooling of her own day: women hadn’t failed at reason, she argued. They had been kept from it.

cards.headline: Wollstonecraft’s Rights of Woman: the big picture
learned: Wollstonecraft: weakness comes from false education
The mind in a gilt cage
Women should learn to reason and support themselves

questions.prompt: In Emile, how did Rousseau say his heroine Sophie should be educated?

options.label: Exactly as Emile is educated
options.rationale: Rousseau said the sexes should not be educated alike.

options.label: To become a philosopher
options.rationale: That was Wollstonecraft’s kind of hope, not Rousseau’s plan.

options.label: Only in history and law
options.rationale: Sophie’s education centers on pleasing Emile.

questions.explanation: Rousseau held that men and women should not be educated alike, and educated Sophie to please Emile.

questions.prompt: Why, according to Wollstonecraft, did women of her time seem less rational than men?

options.label: Nature gave women weaker minds than men
options.rationale: She argued the weakness was manufactured.

options.label: Schooling trained them to please, not to reason
Women took no interest in public questions
options.rationale: She blamed their education, not their interests.

options.label: The law forbade women from reading books
options.rationale: Her target was education, not a reading ban.

questions.explanation: She blamed a false system of education that made women alluring rather than rational.

questions.prompt: Wollstonecraft argued character comes from education, not birth. Which Level 6 idea also made goodness something earned rather than inherited?

options.label: Plato’s Form of Justice
options.rationale: That’s about what is real, not how you become good.

options.label: Laozi’s wu wei, acting without forcing
options.rationale: That’s about acting naturally, not earning a title.

options.label: Nagasena’s chariot of parts
options.rationale: That’s about the self, not goodness.

questions.explanation: Confucius helped turn junzi from a prince’s son into a title of moral nobility anyone could earn.
